# ffibox: the shared seam's contract for a C object that locks itself

Status: `open`: the change is ffibox `2ce020f` on `libgit2-crustify/evolution/ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking`, made on
2026-11-14 at the user's direction after the triage of open proposals, awaiting its review.

Goal: Safety, its soundness measure; ffibox's G9 and G12.

## Signal

Two ffibox documents disagree (`evolution` §2, "skills that contradict each other", here a
tool's docs). `CCell::ref_from_ptr` (`src/traits.rs`, at `9c22a73`), which
`CRefSeam::from_ptr` forwards to, requires that "nothing may write it while the handle
lives except through a `Mut` derived from the same borrow". `docs/ownership.md`'s
shared-and-mutable table puts "routines that lock internally" on `FooRef`. The macro's own
`CCell` safety comment, "`$rf` has no write operation", says the same as the trait.

A C object that serializes its own state, such as glibc's `FILE`, whose every stdio
routine writes its buffer under the stream's recursive lock, cannot meet the trait's
wording. C writes such an object while a `FooRef` lives, on another thread too, and that
is exactly what the table allows. Wave 2 of glibc-crustify binds `FILE` opaque, as
`File`/`FileRef`, and states the contract for a stream on the type
(`src/libc/libio/genops.rs`): the stream stays open for `'a`, and whatever else writes it
does so under its lock, while the handle reads nothing without the lock. That is the
table's meaning, but it is not the trait's text.

## Destination

ffibox: `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s `# Safety` section, and the `CCell` safety comment
`define_ctype!` emits.

## Change

`ref_from_ptr`'s contract reads: "`ptr` must address a live, initialised `Self::C` (or be
null) that outlives `'a`, and nothing may write it while the handle lives except through a
`Mut` derived from the same borrow, or under a synchronization every operation reachable
through `Self::Ref` takes too (an object that locks itself, whose shared handle reads
nothing without its lock)." The macro's comment says that `$rf` has no write operation of
ffibox's.

Added by the module pass, wave-2/batch-1/run-1 (2026-11-13): the shared seam's pointer
needs the same exception. `CRefSeam::as_ptr` (`src/traits.rs:1038`, at `9c22a73`) is
documented as a "Read-only pointer to the C object, for FFI calls taking `*const C`". The
routines that the table puts on `FooRef` take a `foo *` and write the object under its
lock: `fprintf(FILE *, …)` is one. `FileRef` is the only handle wave 3's `fprintf` binding
can take, and it passes the stream as `stream.as_ptr().cast_mut()`. That pointer carries
the write provenance of the one C handed to `from_ptr`, but the binding still writes through
a pointer ffibox calls read-only. `as_ptr`'s documentation adds: "or for C routines that
write the object under a lock they take themselves, which `Self::Ref`'s contract allows."
The module pass judged `File`'s thread-safety claim against these documents
(`crustify/reviews/modules/libc/libio/genops.c/wave-2/batch-1/contracts/ffi_import/file-ref-contract-trusts-glibc-locking/report.md`),
and found the self-locking shape that `docs/ownership.md` gives sound for `FILE`, whose
recursive lock rules out `CGuarded`. Both text changes widen what a producer may claim of a
shared handle. A review should mark them as relaxing ffibox's stated contract to match its
own table, rather than as a new permission.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands:

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| the shared handle's contract allows writes under a synchronization every operation reachable through the handle takes, and `as_ptr` serves C routines that write under their own lock | `glibc-crustify`, `ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking` | ffibox `2ce020f` | three runs put self-locking routines on a shared handle, as `docs/ownership.md` allows, against a trait contract that forbade every write | a `contracts` finding on a shared handle of a self-locking object whose binding the trait's text forbids, or a `ub` finding of the `assumed-locking` pattern on one | watched |

## Validation

A documentation change. No reproducer: no current consumer's soundness changes.
Wave 3 (`wave-3/batch-0/run-1`) now relies on it as the module pass foresaw:
`FileRef::print` passes `stream.as_ptr().cast_mut()` to `flockfile`, `fprintf` and
`funlockfile` (`src/libc/stdio_common/fprintf.rs`), each of which writes the stream under
its lock.

## Review

# Goals

ffibox is one vocabulary for every value that crosses the boundary between
Rust and a foreign language, in both directions: memory the foreign side
allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust (**inbound**),
and memory Rust owns that the foreign side holds, calls or reads
(**outbound**). The foreign language is C, as G8 states.

Two parties use each primitive:

- a **producer** implements its unsafe internals: a policy, a layout type, a
  seam, an export. A producer may be a human, an agent or a static analysis
  tool;
- a **consumer** uses it through its safe API, without knowing whether C or
  Rust sits behind it.

ffibox is needed only where the foreign side **aliases** a value: keeps a
pointer to it beyond a call, frees it, or shares its refcount or lock. A
pointer passed down for the duration of one call, and memory the foreign side
never sees, are plain Rust: `&mut`, `&`, `Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`.

The goals below are grouped by what they serve. Each states what it means and
how it is checked.

## Familiarity

### G1. Mirror standard Rust

Each primitive mirrors a standard Rust one a Rust programmer already knows:
`CBox` is `Box`, `CArc` is `Arc`, `CVec` is `Vec`, `CGuard` is `MutexGuard`,
`FooRef` / `FooMut` are `&` / `&mut`. Where a foreign convention has no
standard counterpart, it is expressed as the closest composition of standard
idioms rather than a new concept: a lock over part of an object is `Arc<T>`
with a `Mutex` field; a refcount that proves sole ownership is
`Arc::get_mut`.

Where ownership allows it, each primitive converts to and from its standard
counterpart (`Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`, `CStr`, `&[T]`) and implements the standard
traits its counterpart does (`Clone`, `Debug`, `Iterator`, `Eq`, `Hash`), so
that a consumer can leave ffibox as soon as the foreign side stops aliasing.

*Checked by:* every primitive names its standard counterpart in its
documentation, and every departure from it states why.

### G2. No more discipline than standard Rust

A consumer needs no more care with a primitive than with its standard
counterpart: no ordering rules, no manual release, no invariants to remember.
In particular, a consumer writes no `unsafe`.

*Checked by:* consumer code, and the tests of the safe interface, compile with
`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

### G3. Continue ffibox's style

New primitives continue the style ffibox has established: its terms (owner,
handle, policy, seam, adopt, surrender), its naming patterns (`C`-prefixed
owners, `Foo` / `FooRef` / `FooMut` per type, `impl_*!` per policy trait) and
its preference for reusing one primitive across cases over adding one per
case. This is a direction, not a freeze: a new term, name or primitive is
welcome where it is clearer than stretching an existing one, and it states
what it adds and how it relates to the terms beside it.

*Checked by:* the documentation's walk from a foreign declaration to its
wrapper stays a short decision table per direction, and each term it uses is
defined once.

## Expressiveness

### G4. Ownership conventions as Rust idioms

A foreign language's ownership conventions are expressed with Rust's own:
`Drop` for release, `Clone` for copies and reference counts, lifetimes for
borrows and keepalive, `&` / `&mut` exclusivity for access, `Send` / `Sync`
for thread affinity, `Pin` for address sensitivity, `Option` for nullability
and slices for cardinality. A convention that one primitive cannot express is
a gap in the vocabulary, not a reason for a raw pointer in the consumer's API.

*Checked by:* the public interface of a binding carries no raw pointer and no
`unsafe fn` except where an obligation cannot be expressed in types, each
such case documented.

### G5. Foreign patterns as Rust patterns

Beyond ownership, a foreign API follows recurring patterns, and each is
expressed as the standard Rust trait or idiom it corresponds to, declared in
the foreign language's own terms: the producer names the foreign routines and
conventions, and the primitive supplies the Rust side.

| foreign pattern | Rust pattern |
|-----------------|--------------|
| a cursor advanced by `next(it)` until NULL or a status; a `count` and `get(i)` pair; a `->next` chain; a sentinel-terminated array | `Iterator`, `IntoIterator`, slices |
| a `foreach(callback, context)` visitor | a closure, or an `Iterator` where the visit can be suspended |
| a status code, `errno`, an error out-parameter | `Result` with a typed error |
| out-parameters | return values |
| a read or write callback pair over a stream | `Read`, `Write`, `Seek` |
| a key-value option setter, a configuration struct filled before use | a builder |
| a struct of function pointers a library calls into | a trait the Rust side implements |

A pattern is one primitive, parameterised by the routines that implement it,
so that every API using it reads the same in Rust. In the outbound direction,
the same primitive offers a Rust iterator, error or trait to the foreign side
in its own convention.

*Checked by:* the public interface of a binding exposes no foreign pattern
whose Rust counterpart exists: no cursor to advance by hand, no status code to
check, no out-parameter to fill.

### G6. Both directions, symmetrically

Every primitive serves both directions with the same terms. Adopting has
surrendering; a policy that binds a foreign routine has an export that offers
a Rust routine to the foreign side; a foreign callback has a Rust closure
behind a foreign function pointer; a foreign global has a Rust static the
foreign side reads. Either side can produce any ownership shape, and either
can consume it.

*Checked by:* every inbound primitive names its outbound counterpart, or
states why it has none.

### G7. Composable axes

Shape (one object, a run, a string), policy (what release, copy and
construction mean), sharing (sole or counted), lock scope, thread affinity,
address sensitivity and element ownership are independent axes. Primitives
compose along them: owners are elements of vectors, fields of
`#[repr(C)]` structs and contents of guards, with no primitive of their own
for each combination.

*Checked by:* a new combination of axes needs no new primitive.

### G8. C first

ffibox targets C. Its names, the `C`-prefixed owners, `c_drop`, `as_c_ptr`,
are C's, and so are the conventions its primitives encode: `malloc` and
`free`, refcounts, C locks, NUL-terminated strings, status codes and `errno`,
callbacks with a context pointer. No primitive is shaped for a language ffibox
does not serve yet: C++'s move constructors, exceptions and smart pointers,
and Go's pointer-passing rules, are out of scope for now.

When another language is taken on, its conventions are added beside C's
rather than folded into them, and what the two share is factored out then,
from what they actually share, without changing what C bindings write.

*Checked by:* every primitive serves a convention a C API uses.

## Safety

### G9. UB hazards excluded by construction

A binding built from the primitives cannot reach undefined behaviour from safe
code. Each hazard is excluded by a primitive or a producer's contract:

| hazard | excluded by |
|--------|-------------|
| aliasing a foreign object through a reference | handles: no Rust reference over foreign memory that anything may write or free while the reference lives (C, another handle, another thread), and no `&mut` over memory anything else may access |
| moving an address-sensitive object | pinned owners; inline values only for movable layouts |
| null dereference | `NonNull`, `Option` with the null niche |
| invalid values (`_Bool`, `char`, out-of-range enums) | plain-element markers, open enums |
| reading uninitialised memory | `MaybeUninit`, construction phases, `assume_init` |
| misalignment | layout types, alignment bounds on copies |
| out-of-bounds access | slices and runs carrying their length |
| type confusion through erased pointers | typed erasure and recovery |
| use after free, outliving a keepalive | lifetimes, counted references |
| double release, release by the wrong routine | policies pairing release with allocation |
| data races | `Send` / `Sync` opt-in, lock scopes |
| re-entrancy through callbacks | callback arguments typed by the access the caller holds |
| unwinding or `longjmp` across the boundary | panic barriers, documented non-local exits |

Leaks are not undefined behaviour and are not excluded, but no primitive leaks
except by an explicit surrender.

*Checked by:* each hazard has a test that the binding's safe interface cannot
reach it, a compile-fail test where the type system rejects it.

### G10. Safe by default

Every default is the conservative one: foreign types are neither `Send` nor
`Sync`, adopting a pointer is `unsafe`, no status code is discarded, and an
unknown fact selects the more restrictive primitive. Every relaxation is an
explicit opt-in that states its justification.

*Checked by:* a binding with no opt-ins is sound, if less capable.

### G11. Failure semantics

No panic crosses into the foreign language: exports and callbacks have a
barrier that maps a panic to the routine's error convention. No foreign unwind
or `longjmp` crosses Rust frames with destructors. Allocation failure is a
value, `Option` or `Result`, never an abort. Teardown that fails or panics
still releases each object exactly once.

*Checked by:* tests that panic in callbacks, exports and drops, under the
sanitizers.

### G12. Unsafe encapsulated, obligations local

`unsafe` stays with producers, in policy implementations, layout types, seams
and exports, and is crate-private to the binding wherever it can be. Every
unsafe trait and seam states a falsifiable `# Safety` contract in terms of the
foreign side's observable behaviour, checkable one implementation at a time,
without reasoning about the whole program. The distinct obligations are few
and listed, so that auditing a binding is a checklist.

*Checked by:* every `unsafe impl` and `unsafe` block maps to one listed
obligation.

### G13. Type safety through traits

Generic code is bound by traits rather than raw pointers: a policy implements
the lifecycle traits for the exact type it releases, a routine of the wrong
type does not compile, erased values are recovered through the trait of the
type they hold, and a family of foreign types generated from one template or
macro shares one generic wrapper.

*Checked by:* compile-fail tests binding a routine, an element or an erased
value to the wrong type.

### G14. A small, verified trusted base

ffibox's own unsafe code is minimal, and exercised under Miri with strict
provenance, the sanitizers and BorrowSanitizer. Each misuse it claims to
prevent has a compile-fail test. Its guarantees are only as strong as this
base.

*Checked by:* the test suite runs clean under each instrument.

## Cost

### G15. Zero overhead

A primitive costs what the equivalent raw code costs. With a stateless policy
an owner is pointer-sized and a handle is one pointer; runtime state is
carried only when the foreign contract needs it, and no check is made that the
foreign contract does not require.

*Checked by:* compile-time size assertions, and benchmarks against raw calls.

### G16. ABI fidelity

A primitive that stands in for a foreign value has a guaranteed ABI:
`#[repr(transparent)]` where it crosses by value, the null pointer as `None`,
the foreign layout where the foreign side reads its fields.

*Checked by:* compile-time size and alignment assertions against the foreign
layout.

Each primitive mirrors a standard Rust one a Rust programmer already knows:

standard counterpart, it is expressed as the closest composition of standard
idioms rather than a new concept: a lock over part of an object is `Arc<T>`
with a `Mutex` field; a refcount that proves sole ownership is

counterpart (`Box`, `Vec`, `Arc`, `CStr`, `&[T]`) and implements the standard

*Checked by:* every primitive names its standard counterpart in its
documentation, and every departure from it states why.

counterpart: no ordering rules, no manual release, no invariants to remember.

welcome where it is clearer than stretching an existing one, and it states
what it adds and how it relates to the terms beside it.

*Checked by:* the documentation's walk from a foreign declaration to its
wrapper stays a short decision table per direction, and each term it uses is
defined once.

|--------|-------------|

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes
  a test or a doctest. A packaging defect's reproducer becomes a test too, run
  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.
- A new tool is drafted and tested where it serves a repeated procedure, preferably as a
  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

A fix that unblocks the campaign, or that would prevent a defect in later campaigns, is
landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

A rerun shows that a change answers the case that exposed it, not that it holds: that is
watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

## 8. Review

Every change is reviewed before it lands, on its evolution branch, by a run other than the
one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks

- the proposal's evidence shows the signal, and the change answers it;

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

# Soundness patterns

The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a
memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here
has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not
what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a
review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one
module met is not met again in the next.

## 1. Patterns

Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated
as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md)
give the routes that do it.

### 1.1 Values the C trusts

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review |
| `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan |
| `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan |
| `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan |

### 1.2 Memory and ownership

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review |
| `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review |
| `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review |
| `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review |
| `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review |
| `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review |
| `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review |
| `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review |

### 1.3 Threads and callbacks

| id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review |
| `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review |
| `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review |

A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names
is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it
whenever one is added.

## 2. Findings

A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A
sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none.

A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise
the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the
catalogue lacks.

## 3. Evolution

The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes:

- a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names,
  with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is
  that campaign's lesson;
- a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the
  findings that escaped it; and
- a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the
  catalogue is for.

What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over
the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the
modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing,
since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken
against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong
the catalogue does not hold yet.

## Conventions

- **Accessors live on the handles.** Getters on `FooRef<'a>` taking `&self`,
  setters on `FooMut<'a>` taking `&mut self`; `FooMut` reaches the getters with
  `as_ref()`, so they are written once. Both project a raw pointer out of the
  handle and read or write through `addr_of!` / `addr_of_mut!`.
- **Every holder reaches the handles the same way:** `as_ref()` / `as_mut()` on
  `Foo`, `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal` and `FooMut` itself (where `as_mut()` is
  the reborrow `&mut` gets implicitly: `helper(m.as_mut())` keeps `m`);
  `as_ref()` on `CArc`, whose exclusive handle comes only from `get_mut()` /
  `make_mut()`; `as_ref()` / `as_locked()` on a `CGuard` and on `FooLocked` (where
  `as_locked()` reborrows). `CSliceMut` reborrows the same
  way, and splits and sub-ranges like `&mut [T]`. Never `Deref`:
  `Deref::Target` cannot name a lifetime taken from `&self`, and since `FooRef`
  is `Copy`, a `Deref<Target = FooRef<'a>>` on `FooMut` would let safe code copy
  a shared handle out while keeping the exclusive one.
- **No reference covers C memory anything may write.** `&FooRef` covers one pointer of Rust stack,
  never the object. The one place a reference covers a C struct's bytes is
  `Foo::as_ref` / `as_mut` on a value Rust holds inline. A run of bytes an
  object lends, a NUL string or a counted run, is lent as `&CStr` or `&[u8]`
  only while nothing writes it, as [Choosing a borrow](#choosing-a-borrow)
  describes; otherwise it is a `CSlice`.
- **The handles' seams are traits the macros implement:** `CRefSeam` on
  `FooRef` (`from_ptr`, `as_ptr` and the `void *` pair), `CMutSeam` on `FooMut`
  (`from_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr` and the `void *` pair) and `CLockedSeam` on
  `FooLocked` (`as_mut_ptr` alone). Import them wherever the seam is used, in
  the crate that invokes `define_ctype!` or in any other that holds its
  handles. Their methods are provided once, by ffibox, so the wrapper crate
  defines no raw-pointer method of its own for them. The inbound half is also
  on `CCell` (`ref_from_ptr`, `mut_from_ptr` and the `void *` twins), so
  generic code over `T: CCell` can borrow a pointer C gives it; those are
  `unsafe`, and the handles' `from_ptr` forward to them. Adopting ownership is
  a different verb on a different type — see
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#conventions).

## Choosing a borrow

Reached when dropping the Rust value does *not* release the object. When it
does, the answer is an owner — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing).

- **No — C, or a parent object, releases it.** Borrow it:
  - one object → `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`, its lifetime tied to whatever
    keeps it alive (a parent's handle, the call);
  - a run of elements → `CSlice<'a, T>` / `CSliceMut<'a, T>`;
  - a counted run of immutable bytes an object lends, `const uint8_t *data`
    with its `size_t len` (from a getter pair, or two fields) → `&'a [u8]`
    from `core::slice::from_raw_parts`, tied to the shared handle's `'a`, as a
    NUL string is a `&CStr`. A run of other `CPlainElem` values is the same
    `&'a [T]`. The SAFETY comment shows, from C's contract, that:
    - nothing writes, moves or frees the bytes while the shared handle lives:
      no routine reachable through a `FooRef` writes, grows or reallocates
      them (not one on `FooRef`, not one on a `FooLocked` taken beside it, not
      another thread's, if `Foo` is `Sync`); a write reachable only through
      `FooMut` is excluded by the borrow;
    - they live as long as the object does, freed with it or with a parent the
      lifetime covers, not by the next call that refills a shared buffer; and
    - `data` addresses `len` initialised bytes in one allocation. A NULL or
      empty run returns `&[]` without the call, since `from_raw_parts` takes
      no NULL even for a length of 0.

    reallocates behind a `const` pointer, or state another thread writes, the
    run is a `CSlice<'a, u8>` built with `CSlice::from_raw_parts`, which forms
    no reference: `elems`, `copy_to_slice` and `to_cvec` copy the bytes out.

    either way: who may write the bytes does. A caller that keeps the bytes
    past the object's borrow takes an owned copy;

    getter;

    typically a C global and the C lock protecting it → `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>`,
    `'static` for a global, with `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`;
  - a NUL string → `&CStr` / `&str` / `&[u8]` tied to the owner's borrow,
    on the terms of a counted byte run above;
  - an out-parameter slot → `&'a mut MaybeUninit<T>` from
    `ptr.cast::<MaybeUninit<T>>().as_mut()`; no ffibox type;

A function pointer is bound from its declaration and every site that calls it or supplies
it, a function assigned to it or passed as it. One a typedef declares is named after its
typedef; one written inline is named after the site that declares it, the field,
parameter, return or global, as the [conventions](../../conventions/SKILL.md)' Naming

It is bound to a safe callable type that holds either of its implementations:

- a Rust closure, which C reaches through a trampoline of the C signature and the context
  C passes back to it; and
- a C function, with its context, which Rust calls: made only inside the crate, through an
  `unsafe` constructor whose contract states what the C that supplies it guarantees, the
  function's validity and its context's lifetime and threads, and safe to call, its
  arguments and result converted as a function's binding converts them.

A function pointer that crosses the boundary gets both, whichever direction its uses take
today, since a port turns the C that calls or supplies it into Rust, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section describes, and its safe API
does not change then. Its consumers see only the safe form, its closures taking and
returning safe types: a closure borrowed for the call, `impl FnMut(…)`, where C keeps it
for the call that receives it; an owned closure, released with its context, where C keeps
it until it releases it; and a trait, for a struct of function pointers a library calls
into, which Rust types and the C implementation implement alike. A function pointer read
from C, such as a field's getter returns, is the callable type, never the raw pointer.
How long C keeps it is a finding of the analysis.

Its trampoline is a panic barrier, which maps a panic to the C's error convention, and it
refuses a re-entrant call, which would alias an `FnMut` closure, unless the analysis shows
that C re-enters it, which takes an `Fn` closure instead. A function pointer C calls from
another thread takes a `Send` closure, and a `Sync` one when C may call it from several at
once. Four cases shape the type further:

- one without a context parameter carries no captured state: its Rust implementation is a
  closure without captures, each closure type its own trampoline, or a plain function;
- one C reads as absent when null, where it uses a default or calls nothing, is an
  `Option` of the callable type;
- one C compares with a known function, such as its default implementation, keeps in its C
  variant the pointer it was made from, so that the comparison still holds; and
- one whose context C reaches through another argument, such as the object it is handed,
  has a C half only for functions sound with any such argument. A C function that reads its
  context there is reached only through the object that holds it, by the routine that
  dispatches it with that object, bound or ported, which calls it through its raw binding,
  and never as the callable type, whose safe call could hand it another object. Such a
  function is stored only from C, or through an `unsafe` setter whose contract carries the
  object's context, and is read back as its address, no callable.

When its sites hand ownership across differently, each distribution has its own distinctly
named callable type over the one C function-pointer type.

# Review of ffibox `2ce020f` (`ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking`)

**Verdict: rejected. Five fixes are required, all small.** The direction is right. The signal is real: at `9c22a73`, `ref_from_ptr`'s `# Safety` contradicts `docs/ownership.md:180`, and wave 3's `FileRef::print` (`53dd776`, `fprintf.rs:116`) passes `stream.as_ptr().cast_mut()` to `flockfile`, `fprintf` and `funlockfile`. Placing the fix in ffibox is right too. But as written, the new text lets safe code reach UB, which I proved under Miri. It also widens a second contract without saying so, and it contradicts a rule it left untouched.

**It weakens a check, and must be marked so.** `ref_from_ptr`'s contract is what a `contracts` review judges every adoption against. The widened text passes adoptions the old text failed, and `as_ptr` is no longer read-only. This is justified: it brings the trait in line with ffibox's own table and with what `CArc::as_ref` already hands out. It corrects the trait rather than granting something new, but the mark stands.

## Required fixes
